title: Azure RBAC vs Azure Policy
summary: Who can do things versus what the end state must look like.

values: Authorization: controls which actions a security principal can perform.
Governance: controls which resource configurations are allowed and reports compliance.
Can this user/identity do this operation here?
Is this resource configured according to our rules?
Management group, subscription, resource group, resource.
Management group, subscription, resource group (with exclusions and exemptions).
Specific principals (users, groups, service principals, managed identities).
All requests and resources in scope, regardless of who makes them — including Owners.
Deny unless a role grants the action.
Allow unless a policy effect (e.g., Deny) blocks or modifies it.
Let developers manage VMs in one RG; give auditors read access.
Allowed regions, allowed VM SKUs, required tags, deploy diagnostics automatically.
Can't restrict property values (e.g., which region) for an allowed action.
Doesn't grant permissions; Deny doesn't remove existing non-compliant resources.
Over-broad roles = privilege escalation risk. Use least privilege and groups.
Enforces guardrails even for privileged users; remediation identities need RBAC roles.
'Allow the help desk to restart VMs but not delete them.'
'Ensure no one can create resources outside West Europe.'

keyDifference: RBAC decides WHO can act. Policy decides WHAT is allowed to exist — for everyone.
memoryAid: RBAC = Role (who). Policy = Property (what). A Contributor can deploy a VM (RBAC), but Policy decides whether that VM may be in Japan East.

examScenarios.scenario: Users with Contributor keep deploying expensive VM sizes. You need to block sizes larger than D4s_v5.
examScenarios.answer: Azure Policy with the 'Allowed virtual machine size SKUs' definition (Deny effect). RBAC can't restrict SKU choice.

examScenarios.scenario: A contractor must be able to view all resources in one resource group and nothing else.
examScenarios.answer: Azure RBAC: assign Reader to the contractor at that resource group scope.

examScenarios.scenario: Every resource must have a CostCenter tag copied from its resource group, including existing resources.
examScenarios.answer: Azure Policy with a Modify effect ('Inherit a tag from the resource group'), plus a remediation task for existing resources.

title: Microsoft Entra Roles vs Azure RBAC Roles
summary: Directory administration versus Azure resource administration.

values: Manage directory objects and tenant settings: users, groups, apps, domains, licenses.
Manage Azure resources: VMs, storage, networks, subscriptions.
Global Administrator, User Administrator, Helpdesk Administrator, Application Administrator.
Owner, Contributor, Reader, User Access Administrator, Virtual Machine Contributor.
Tenant, administrative unit, or specific app registration.
Management group, subscription, resource group, resource.
Entra admin center / Microsoft Graph.
Azure portal Access control (IAM) / Azure Resource Manager.
Supported for some permission sets (requires Entra ID P1/P2).
Supported with JSON role definitions and assignable scopes.
No access to Azure resources by default — even Global Administrator.
No ability to manage users, groups or tenant settings.
Global Administrator can elevate to User Access Administrator at root scope — monitor and minimize.
Owner and User Access Administrator can grant access — tightly control them; use PIM.
'Allow a user to reset passwords for users in the Sales department only.'
'Allow a user to manage virtual networks in RG-Net.'

keyDifference: Entra roles manage identities in the directory. RBAC roles manage resources in subscriptions. They meet only through 'elevate access'.
memoryAid: Entra = Everyone's identity. RBAC = Resources. If the task touches a user object, think Entra; if it touches a VM, think RBAC.

examScenarios.scenario: A Global Administrator can't see any subscriptions in the portal.
examScenarios.answer: Enable 'Access management for Azure resources' to elevate to User Access Administrator at root scope, then assign the needed RBAC role.

examScenarios.scenario: The London help desk must reset passwords only for London users.
examScenarios.answer: Create an administrative unit for London users and assign the Helpdesk Administrator Entra role scoped to it.

title: LRS vs ZRS vs GRS vs GZRS
summary: Choose storage redundancy by the failure you must survive.

values: 3 copies in one datacenter.
3 copies across 3 availability zones.
3 in one primary datacenter + 3 (LRS) in the paired region.
3 across zones in primary + 3 (LRS) in the paired region.
Drive, server or rack failure.
Loss of a datacenter/zone.
Loss of the primary region (after failover).
Zone loss and loss of the primary region.
None.
None.
Asynchronous.
Asynchronous.
N/A
N/A
Only with RA-GRS (or after failover).
Only with RA-GZRS (or after failover).
Lowest.
Higher than LRS.
Higher than ZRS.
Highest.
No protection from datacenter or zone outage.
No regional disaster protection; not in every region.
Primary not zone-redundant; async = possible data loss (RPO).
Not available in every region; async geo replication.
Supported.
Supported.
Not supported.
Not supported.
Dev/test data or data that can be recreated, at minimum cost.
High availability if a zone fails; data must stay in region.
Recover from a regional disaster at lower cost.
Maximum durability; read access during regional outages with RA-GZRS.

keyDifference: L = one Location (datacenter), Z = Zones, G = Geo (second region). Add RA- to read the secondary.
memoryAid: Think of the letters as layers: LRS ⊂ ZRS (spread across zones), then add G for a second region. GZRS = ZRS + GRS's geo copy. 'RA' = Read Access.

examScenarios.scenario: An app must keep reading blob data if the primary region is unavailable, without waiting for a failover.
examScenarios.answer: RA-GRS or RA-GZRS — read from the secondary endpoint.

examScenarios.scenario: Data must remain available if a single datacenter fails, and must not leave the region.
examScenarios.answer: ZRS.

examScenarios.scenario: Cheapest redundancy for scratch analytics data.
examScenarios.answer: LRS.

versionNote: Regional availability of ZRS/GZRS and supported conversions change over time.

title: Azure Files vs Azure Blob Storage
summary: Mountable file shares versus object storage.

values: Fully managed file shares (SMB, NFS).
Massively scalable object storage for unstructured data.
Mount as a drive / file system (SMB 3.x over TCP 445, NFS 4.1); also REST.
HTTPS REST API, SDKs, AzCopy, Storage Explorer; NFS 3.0 and SFTP optional; Data Lake Gen2 (hierarchical namespace).
True directories and files with file locks and ACLs.
Flat namespace of containers and blobs (virtual folders), unless hierarchical namespace is enabled.
Identity-based SMB auth (AD DS, Entra Domain Services, Entra Kerberos) + share RBAC + NTFS ACLs.
Entra ID with data roles, SAS, account keys; container-level anonymous access (optional).
Premium (SSD), transaction optimized, hot, cool.
Hot, cool, cold, archive per blob.
Lift-and-shift file servers, shared app config, Azure File Sync, container volumes.
Images and video, backups, data lakes, static website content, logs.
Port 445 often blocked over the internet; share size limits.
No SMB mounting; archive tier is offline.
'Replace an on-premises file server and keep NTFS permissions.'
'Store millions of images at the lowest cost and move old ones to archive automatically.'

keyDifference: Files is a network file share you mount; Blob is object storage you call over HTTP.
memoryAid: Files = Folders you mount. Blob = Big Lots Of Bytes over HTTP.

examScenarios.scenario: Legacy app on several VMs needs a shared drive letter.
examScenarios.answer: Azure Files (SMB share mounted on each VM).

examScenarios.scenario: Keep log files for 7 years at minimal cost; rarely read.
examScenarios.answer: Blob storage with a lifecycle policy moving blobs to archive.

examScenarios.scenario: Branch servers need local caching of a central share.
examScenarios.answer: Azure Files + Azure File Sync with cloud tiering.

title: Availability Set vs Availability Zone
summary: Rack-level resilience in one datacenter versus datacenter-level resilience across a region.

values: Spread VMs across fault and update domains within a datacenter.
Spread VMs across physically separate datacenters (zones) in a region.
Rack/hardware failure; planned maintenance reboots.
Entire datacenter failure (power, cooling, network), plus hardware failure.
One datacenter.
One region (3+ zones).
Lowest (same datacenter).
Slightly higher (different buildings), still low.
High VM SLA for 2+ VMs in a set.
Highest VM SLA for 2+ VMs across zones.
No datacenter-level protection; VM must be placed at creation.
Not in every region; needs zone-redundant supporting services (Standard LB/IP).
'Ensure VMs aren't all rebooted together during maintenance in a region without zones.'
'Ensure the app survives a datacenter failure.'

keyDifference: Sets separate racks; zones separate buildings.
memoryAid: SET = Same building, Even Trays (racks). ZONE = Zero shared building.

examScenarios.scenario: You must achieve the highest SLA for a two-VM web tier.
examScenarios.answer: Deploy the VMs in two different availability zones behind a Standard Load Balancer.

examScenarios.scenario: A region doesn't support zones; protect against a single rack failure.
examScenarios.answer: Use an availability set.

title: Container Instances vs Container Apps vs App Service
summary: Three ways to run containers without managing VMs.

values: Run a container or group quickly, no orchestration.
Serverless microservices and event-driven apps.
Managed web apps and APIs (code or containers).
Manual — set CPU/memory per group; create more groups to scale.
Automatic (HTTP, CPU, KEDA events) including scale to zero.
Manual or autoscale on the App Service plan (Standard+).
Per second of CPU/memory.
Consumption (per use) or dedicated workload profiles.
Per App Service plan instance.
Public IP/DNS label or VNet deployment.
Environment can be VNet-integrated; built-in ingress.
Access restrictions, VNet integration (outbound), private endpoints (inbound).
Batch jobs, build agents, simple tasks.
APIs, background processors, microservices with revisions and traffic splitting.
Websites and APIs needing slots, custom domains, TLS.
No autoscaling; limited orchestration.
No direct Kubernetes API access.
Web-centric; not for arbitrary background workloads at scale.
'Run a nightly container job with minimal cost and setup.'
'Scale a container API to zero when idle.'
'Swap staging and production with zero downtime.'

keyDifference: ACI = single containers on demand; ACA = autoscaling microservices; App Service = web apps with slots.
memoryAid: ACI is a taxi (one ride, on demand). ACA is a bus network (routes, scales with riders). App Service is a hotel for websites (rooms, staging areas).

examScenarios.scenario: A container job runs once a day for 10 minutes and must not incur cost otherwise.
examScenarios.answer: Azure Container Instances with restart policy Never/OnFailure (or a Container Apps job).

examScenarios.scenario: An event-driven processor should scale with queue length and scale to zero.
examScenarios.answer: Azure Container Apps with a KEDA queue scale rule and min replicas 0.

title: Network Security Group vs Azure Firewall
summary: Distributed L3/L4 filtering versus a centralized, stateful firewall service.

values: Allow/deny traffic to subnets and NICs by 5-tuple.
Central network security service with stateful inspection and threat intelligence.
Layers 3–4 (IP, port, protocol).
Layers 3–7: network rules, application rules (FQDN/HTTP(S)), DNAT.
Per subnet or NIC, within one region.
Deployed in a hub VNet (AzureFirewallSubnet); traffic steered via UDRs; can protect many VNets.
IPs, ranges, service tags, ASGs, ports.
FQDNs and FQDN tags, web categories (Premium), TLS inspection and IDPS (Premium), threat-intel-based filtering.
No charge.
Hourly deployment charge + data processed.
No FQDN filtering, no centralized logging of decisions beyond flow logs.
Requires routing (UDRs) and a dedicated subnet; cost.
Good micro-segmentation; rules sprawl across many NSGs.
Central policy, logging and egress control; single choke point to secure outbound.
'Only allow the web subnet to reach the DB subnet on 1433.'
'Allow VMs to reach only *.windowsupdate.com on the internet.'

keyDifference: NSGs filter by IP/port where traffic lands; Azure Firewall inspects and filters centrally, including by FQDN.
memoryAid: NSG = door lock on each room. Firewall = security checkpoint at the building entrance that also reads names (FQDNs).

examScenarios.scenario: Restrict outbound internet access from all spokes to a list of approved domains.
examScenarios.answer: Azure Firewall application rules in the hub, with UDR 0.0.0.0/0 → firewall private IP on spoke subnets.

examScenarios.scenario: Block RDP into a subnet from everywhere except the management subnet.
examScenarios.answer: NSG inbound rules on the subnet.

title: Service Endpoint vs Private Endpoint
summary: Secure the public endpoint to your subnet, or bring the service onto a private IP.

values: Extend subnet identity to an Azure service over the backbone.
Give a specific resource a private IP in your VNet via Private Link.
Service's public endpoint/public IP.
Private IP of a NIC in your subnet.
Whole service type per subnet (e.g., all storage accounts), unless service endpoint policies are used.
One specific resource and sub-resource.
Not for on-premises traffic.
Yes — from peered VNets and on-premises over VPN/ExpressRoute.
None.
Required — privatelink private DNS zone or custom DNS.
Free.
Per endpoint-hour and per GB processed.
Public endpoint remains; exfiltration to other accounts possible without endpoint policies.
Public access can be disabled; access limited to the mapped resource.
'Allow only VMs in Subnet1 to access the storage account, at no extra cost.'
'On-premises servers must access the storage account over ExpressRoute using a private IP.'

keyDifference: Service endpoint: your subnet goes to the service. Private endpoint: the service comes to your subnet.
memoryAid: Private endpoint = a Private door with its own address. Service endpoint = a VIP lane to the Service's public front door.

examScenarios.scenario: Disable all public network access to an Azure SQL server but keep access from a VNet.
examScenarios.answer: Private endpoint for the SQL server, then disable public network access.

examScenarios.scenario: A subnet needs access to storage accounts and you want the cheapest solution; on-premises access isn't needed.
examScenarios.answer: Service endpoint (Microsoft.Storage) on the subnet plus a VNet rule on each storage firewall.

title: Azure Load Balancer vs Application Gateway
summary: Layer 4 flow distribution versus Layer 7 HTTP(S) routing.

values: Distribute TCP/UDP flows across healthy backends.
Route and protect HTTP(S) web traffic.
Layer 4 (transport).
Layer 7 (application).
5-tuple hash (or client IP affinity).
Host name, URL path, headers; redirects and rewrites.
Passes encrypted traffic through; no termination.
TLS termination and end-to-end TLS.
Relies on NSGs; no WAF.
Web Application Firewall (WAF_v2).
Regional; public or internal; no dedicated subnet required.
Regional; requires a dedicated subnet.
Non-HTTP apps, internal tiers, NVA HA ports.
Websites, multi-site hosting, path-based routing, WAF protection.
'Load-balance RDP/SQL/custom TCP traffic across VMs.'
'Send /images/* to one pool and /api/* to another.'

keyDifference: Load Balancer looks at IPs and ports; Application Gateway reads the HTTP request.
memoryAid: Load Balancer reads the envelope (IP and port, Layer 4). Application Gateway opens the letter (URL, host header, cookies, Layer 7).

examScenarios.scenario: Protect a web app from SQL injection and route by URL path.
examScenarios.answer: Application Gateway with WAF_v2 and a path-based rule.

examScenarios.scenario: Provide a private VIP for a SQL Server Always On listener.
examScenarios.answer: Internal Standard Load Balancer.

title: VPN Gateway vs ExpressRoute
summary: Encrypted tunnels over the internet versus a private provider circuit.

values: Public internet (encrypted IPsec/IKE or SSL tunnels).
Private connection through a connectivity provider.
Encrypted by default.
Not encrypted by default (MACsec on ExpressRoute Direct or IPsec over ER can be added).
Limited by gateway SKU and internet conditions; variable latency.
Higher bandwidth options with predictable latency.
Hours (gateway deployment can take 45+ minutes).
Days to weeks (provider provisioning).
Site-to-site, point-to-site, VNet-to-VNet.
Site/datacenter connectivity only (no individual clients).
Lower: gateway hours + egress.
Higher: circuit + provider + gateway.
Internet-dependent performance.
Not encrypted by default; requires provider; longer lead time.
'Connect a branch office quickly and cheaply.' / 'Remote admins from home.'
'Traffic must not traverse the internet and needs consistent latency.'

keyDifference: VPN = encrypted over the internet; ExpressRoute = private, not over the internet.
memoryAid: VPN is a Very Private tunnel on a Public Network. ExpressRoute is your own Express lane that never touches the public road.

examScenarios.scenario: Provide failover if the ExpressRoute circuit goes down.
examScenarios.answer: Configure a site-to-site VPN as a backup path (both gateways coexist in GatewaySubnet; VPN must be route-based).

examScenarios.scenario: Ten developers need access to Azure VNets from home.
examScenarios.answer: Point-to-site VPN.

title: Azure Monitor Metrics vs Logs
summary: Lightweight numeric time series versus rich, queryable records.

values: Numeric values at regular intervals with dimensions.
Records/events with many properties of different types.
Platform metrics collected automatically.
Need diagnostic settings, agents (AMA + DCR) or app SDKs.
Near real time — ideal for fast alerts.
Minutes of ingestion latency is typical.
Metrics explorer (aggregate, split, filter).
Log Analytics with KQL (join, parse, summarize).
Platform metrics: 93 days.
Configurable per workspace/table, plus long-term archive.
CPU, memory, request counts, latency charts and alerts.
Troubleshooting, auditing, correlation, security analysis.
'Alert within a minute when CPU > 90%.'
'Find which user deleted a resource and correlate with failed sign-ins.'

keyDifference: Metrics tell you THAT something changed (numbers). Logs tell you WHAT happened (details).
memoryAid: Metrics = Measurements on a dashboard gauge. Logs = a detailed diary you search with KQL.

examScenarios.scenario: Query failed requests for the last 24 hours grouped by client IP.
examScenarios.answer: Logs — a KQL query in Log Analytics.

examScenarios.scenario: Chart a storage account's transactions over the last week.
examScenarios.answer: Metrics explorer.

title: Azure Backup vs Azure Site Recovery
summary: Point-in-time data recovery versus workload failover.

values: Protect data: restore files, disks or VMs to a previous point in time.
Business continuity: keep apps running by failing over to another region/site.
Scheduled backups retained per policy (daily, weekly, monthly, yearly).
Continuous replication with frequent recovery points.
RPO = time since last backup (hours); RTO = restore time (minutes–hours).
RPO typically seconds–minutes; RTO minutes via orchestrated failover.
Long-term (years) for compliance.
Short (recovery point retention measured in hours/days).
Accidental deletion, corruption, ransomware.
Regional outages and site disasters.
Recovery Services vault / Backup vault, backup policies.
Recovery Services vault, replication policies, recovery plans, test failover.
'Restore a deleted file from last week.'
'Bring the app online in another region within 30 minutes of an outage.'

keyDifference: Backup brings back data; Site Recovery brings back the running service.
memoryAid: Backup = Back in time. Site Recovery = Somewhere else, right now.

examScenarios.scenario: Validate the DR plan quarterly without affecting production.
examScenarios.answer: Site Recovery test failover into an isolated VNet.

examScenarios.scenario: Keep monthly recovery points for seven years.
examScenarios.answer: Azure Backup policy with monthly/yearly retention.
